title: Who changed my table? Excel launches AI change history to track what was changed and what went wrong in one sentence

content_html:
Microsoft introduces the Change History feature for Excel, designed for tracking modifications in collaborative workbooks. Users can see in the official blog post that Excel workbooks often keep changing due to data updates, evolving requirements, and simultaneous editing by multiple people. Over time, teams often struggle to quickly determine when a piece of data was changed, who made the change, and whether the change affected other calculations.

Ask Copilot a natural language question to sort out the changes

Change History reads existing edit records in Excel and generates modification descriptions using Copilot's reasoning capabilities. Users can directly ask questions in natural language to understand important changes that occurred in a specific time period. This feature summarizes specific modification content, the impact of the changes, and the relevant editors.

In addition, this feature uses different colors to mark user edits and Copilot-assisted modifications, allowing team members to quickly identify whether an anomaly comes from manual operations or AI-assisted changes. The original text did not disclose performance parameters such as the longest historical追溯 period supported by this feature, the scale of workbooks it can handle, and response time.

Rollback can precisely target "an AI change by a person" and also detect formula anomalies

Microsoft also demonstrated a more granular rollback capability: users can ask Copilot to undo a change made by a collaborator with AI assistance, while keeping the collaborator's manual edits that were done independently.

When an Excel formula becomes abnormal, Copilot can also help users analyze which recent changes may have caused the formula to fail. This capability connects formula troubleshooting with the workbook's modification history, reducing the need for users to manually compare numerous cells and version records.
